summary: Defines a frame of reference as the coordinate system used to describe motion, distinguishes inertial frames (not accelerating, Newton's laws hold directly) from non-inertial frames (accelerating, requiring fictitious forces like centrifugal/Coriolis), and notes that Earth is only approximately inertial.
title: 13.1 Frame of Reference

topicTitle: 13.2 Postulates of the Special Theory of Relativity
summary: States Einstein's two postulates of Special Relativity: (1) the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and (2) the speed of light in vacuum is constant for all observers regardless of source or observer motion, then explains why constancy of c forces space and time to become relative (time dilation, length contraction, relativity of simultaneity).
title: Postulates of the Special Theory of Relativity

topicTitle: 13.3 Consequences of Special Theory of Relativity
summary: Covers the consequences of Special Relativity: relativity of simultaneity, time dilation (t = t0/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2)), length contraction (L = L0*sqrt(1-v^2/c^2)), relativistic mass increase (m = m0/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2)), and mass-energy equivalence (E = mc^2), all becoming significant near the speed of light.
title: 13.3 Consequences of Special Theory of Relativity

summary: Explains that Einstein's relativity unified the 3 spatial dimensions and time into a single 4D spacetime framework, since any event requires 4 coordinates (3 spatial + 1 temporal) to be uniquely specified, covers the spacetime interval as an invariant quantity, and traces the historical development from Minkowski's geometric interpretation of Special Relativity.
title: Time as the Fourth Dimension
